text: Lesson 35's load used if_exists equals replace, so every single run wipes the table and reloads all twenty rows. That's fine today. This lesson is about why it stops being fine once a source has millions of rows and the pipeline runs every hour.

Re-extracting and re-loading everything, every run, wastes time and resources on data that hasn't changed since last time. At twenty rows nobody notices. At scale, it's the difference between a pipeline that finishes in seconds and one that takes hours for no reason.

A watermark is just the highest value of an ordering column — usually a date — that's already been successfully loaded. orders.csv has a real column built for exactly this, order_date, and the highest value right now is January 19th, 2026. We persist that watermark in a plain text file between runs — no prior run means start from 1900 and load everything.

extract_incremental reads the CSV with parse_dates on order_date, so pandas treats it as a real datetime instead of plain text, then filters to only rows after the stored watermark. That parse_dates argument matters — without it, the greater-than comparison would be comparing strings, not dates.

Here's the detail that actually matters: the watermark only advances after the load succeeds. run_incremental_pipeline extracts the new rows, cleans them using Lesson 34's logic, loads them using Lesson 35's warehouse function, and only then writes the new watermark. Update it before the load, and a failed run would silently skip those rows forever, believing they were already in.
Watermarks solve re-running too much data. Next lesson solves a different problem: what happens when the same rows get loaded twice anyway, and how to make that safe.
